metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
The structural floor, not the electrical service, is often the first hard limit when retrofitting a building for liquid-cooled AI racks.

Floor loading limits measure the weight a raised floor or slab supports per square foot against the weight actually installed. Liquid-cooled AI racks carry coolant, manifolds, and batteries, so they are far heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. The expectation was that electrical capacity would bind first. In retrofit work, structural limits arrive first more often than the industry expected.

That matters for AI because compute scaling depends on putting racks into buildings. If the slab or raised floor cannot carry the load, available power does not resolve the problem. The building shell becomes a gate on where AI capacity can be added, and capacity planning that tracks only power and space will misjudge what a given site can hold.

What the data does not give is any threshold, any count of affected buildings, or any cost and schedule figure. It describes a limit to be checked building by building rather than a fleet-wide number. The sibling metrics, server utilization rate and stranded power and space per cabinet, cover how installed capacity is used and how much power and space sit idle. This metric speaks only to whether the structure can bear the weight at all.

siblings.label: Stranded power and space per cabinet
